stand up.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

step back.example: Charlie watched Manfred step back into the side hall and swiftly close the door.
step back.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

straighten up.meaning: To stand straight again after bending.
straighten up.example: Manfred had straightened up, but Eustacia sat in a confused silence, gazing at the table.
straighten up.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

swing around.example: Dagbert swung around and snapped, "What do you want?"
swing around.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

take a deep breath.meaning: To breathe in a lot of air, often before doing something hard.
take a deep breath.example: Taking a deep breath, Charlie tiptoed down the creaking stairs as fast as he could.
take a deep breath.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

take a step back.example: The group took a step back, then another.
take a step back.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

take care.meaning: Be careful (said when you say goodbye).
take care.example: You take care now, Charlie," Cook whispered as she closed the door behind him.
take care.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

take off.meaning: (1) To remove clothes. (2) (Of a bird) To leave the ground and fly ("the bird took off from the shuddering treetop"). (3) "Take yourself off to bed" = go to bed ("Charlie took himself off to bed"). (4) "Taken off guard" = surprised.
take off.example: He took off his new glasses and rubbed the lenses with his thumb.
take off.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

take out.meaning: (1) To remove something from a bag or pocket. (2) "Take the spring out of your step" = make you feel less happy ("that didn't take the spring out of Olivia's step").
take out.example: Officer Singh took out his notebook.
take out.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

take over.meaning: (1) To continue something that someone else started. (2) To take control of someone or something ("allow herself to be TAKEN OVER").
take over.example: Tancred took over from Paton and told his father he would be home in the morning.
take over.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

take place.example: Everywhere he looked, a savage fight was taking place.
take place.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

taken aback.example: Gabriel was momentarily taken aback by Dagbert's sharp tone.
taken aback.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

tamper with.meaning: To change or damage something secretly, so that it does harm.
tamper with.example: Don't want anyone tampering with your globe," he said.
tamper with.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

the corner of his eye.meaning: (From the corner of his eye) Seeing something at the side, without looking straight at it.
the corner of his eye.example: But while he collected handfuls of slopping ice, Joshua was watching Dagbert out of the corner of his eye.
the corner of his eye.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

the following day.example: The following day, Lyell Bone and Paton Yewbeam took the box of papers to Lysander's father, Judge Sage.
the following day.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

the rest of.example: Charlie tore down the rest of the steps, stumbling and slipping on the rocky surface.
the rest of.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

the worse for wear.meaning: Damaged, dirty or tired after a hard time.
the worse for wear.example: The outfit looked somewhat the worse for wear.
the worse for wear.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

there there.meaning: Kind words you say to calm someone who is sad or upset. It is not about a place.
there there.example: "There, there, my dear. It's all over now."
there there.usageNote: Informal. Said in a gentle, kind way.

to his surprise.meaning: In a way that surprised him.
to his surprise.example: He found, to his surprise, that he was still running.
to his surprise.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

turn away.meaning: To turn so that you are not facing someone.
turn away.example: Gabriel was about to turn away when he saw two figures coming down the hall behind Manfred.
turn away.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

turn into.meaning: (1) To go into a place by turning. (2) To change and become something else.
turn into.example: Alice said quietly, "Or the sound of a fly turning into something much larger."
turn into.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

turn out.meaning: (1) To happen or end in a particular way. (2) "Turns out" = it is found that ("Turns out she's an illusionist").
turn out.example: If he had locked the door, things might have turned out differently.
turn out.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

turn over.meaning: (1) To move something so that the other side faces up, often while searching. (2) To roll your body onto its other side in bed ("Charlie turned over and closed his eyes").
turn over.example: They rummaged under my counter, turned over the cash register, and then started in here.
turn over.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

turn up.meaning: (1) To arrive; to appear. (2) To find something ("It's quite incredible what you can turn up these days"). (3) To make a sound louder.
turn up.example: I suppose I could turn up and give everyone a fright," he said.
turn up.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

up and down.meaning: Backward and forward; along the whole length of something.
up and down.example: Tancred looked up and down the street.
up and down.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

used to.meaning: (1) "Was used to do something" = was used for doing it ("the ladder that was used to reach the highest shelves"). (2) Did something regularly in the past, but not now. (3) "Be used to" something = know it well so it does not seem strange ("I'm just not used to seeing this young man").
used to.example: I'm just not used to seeing this young man with a mustache."
used to.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

wait for.meaning: To stay until someone comes or something happens.
wait for.example: He frowned with concentration while the others waited for him to continue.
wait for.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

wake up.example: She resolved to wake up very early and set off for Darkly Wynd.
wake up.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

what on earth.meaning: Said to show great surprise, like "what?".
what on earth.example: Bertha, what on earth are you doing?"
what on earth.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

what's going on.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

who on earth.meaning: Said to show great surprise, like "who?".
who on earth.example: But who on earth would believe him?
who on earth.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

work out.meaning: (1) To understand something by thinking. (2) To make a plan ("work out some kind of strategy"). (3) To do exercise.
work out.example: What those arrangements might be, nobody could work out just yet.
work out.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

would rather.example: It thinned and lifted, revealing something they would rather not have seen.
would rather.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

you'd better.meaning: You should (or something bad will happen).
you'd better.example: You'd better stay in here, Billy," Charlie said.
you'd better.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

in charge.meaning: Having the job of looking after something.
in charge.example: My parents said that he was in charge.

deal with.meaning: To take action about a problem.
deal with.example: We'll have to deal with it.

out of earshot.example: When the twins were out of earshot, Emma said, "Something's wrong with Liv."

on the warpath.meaning: Angry and looking for someone to scold.

wrong end of the stick.meaning: A wrong idea about what someone meant.
wrong end of the stick.example: He sometimes got the wrong end of the stick.

rooted to the spot.meaning: Unable to move because of surprise or fear.
rooted to the spot.example: He stood rooted to the spot, scarcely able to believe his eyes.

chain mail.meaning: Armor made of small metal rings.
chain mail.example: The knight was dressed from head to foot in glittering chain mail.

bit of a state.example: Benjamin explained that he had gone to number nine and found Maisie in a "bit of a state," as he put it.

paragraphs.context: An endowed girl whose gift is the ability to bewitch clothes.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Dorcas Loom can put spells on clothes.
paragraphs.simple: This is from the list of endowed children at the start of the book. Dorcas can bewitch clothes, so that the person who wears them is under a spell.

background.note: The children at Bloor's with magic powers from the Red King. Here 'endowed' means 'born with a magic gift'.

paragraphs.context: The Red King arrived in the North nine hundred years ago.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The prologue tells the story so far.
paragraphs.simple: The Red King was an African magician. His ten children each got a little of his power, and their families still live in the city. Some use their powers for evil, and Charlie tries to stop them.

background.note: A magician-king who came out of Africa long ago. All the endowed children are descended from his ten children.

paragraphs.context: Charlie's parents are on their second honeymoon.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Charlie misses his parents, and the city is dangerous.
paragraphs.simple: Charlie's parents have been away at sea for more than a month. They send postcards, but Charlie wishes they would come home. One of his friends was almost drowned.

background.note: A café on Frog Street run by Mr. Onimous. Only people with pets are allowed in.

paragraphs.context: If only the Red King could return to keep the city safe.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Red King is now a tree in his old castle.
paragraphs.simple: Deep in the ruins of his castle, the Red King's heart still beats inside a tall red tree. He sees through the eyes of birds and hears through the ears of animals, but he has little power now. (The end of this paragraph is missing in this copy.)

paragraphs.context: "Menaced," muttered Orvil Onimous.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mr. Onimous feels in danger.
paragraphs.simple: Mr. Onimous hurries through the dark city with his three Flame cats. He says they are "menaced", which means they are in danger. His café has been closed.

background.note: Orvil Onimous, a small furry-looking man who runs the Pets' Café and does pest control with the Flame cats.

paragraphs.context: "Well, he did, in a sense," Tancred agreed.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Tancred is alive, but secretly.
paragraphs.simple: Everyone thinks Dagbert drowned Tancred, and in a way he did. Emma saved him just in time. Tancred sits in the café stroking Sagittarius, one of the Flames.

background.note: A quiet art student with long blond hair. She is endowed: she can turn into a bird and fly.
An endowed art student with crackling blond hair. He is a storm-bringer: his moods make wind, rain and thunder.
One of the three Flame cats. He is yellow like flame.

paragraphs.context: A cold shudder ran down Tancred's spine.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Tancred thinks about the evil at the academy.
paragraphs.simple: In three years at Bloor's Academy, Tancred always felt that Ezekiel and his helpers could do something very evil. When Dagbert the drowner came, the evil finally showed itself.

background.note: A new boy at Bloor's who wears sea-gold charms. He is the son of Lord Grimwald and is a 'drowner'.
Dr. Bloor's very old, evil grandfather. He lives in the west wing of the academy and uses dark magic.

paragraphs.context: The swordsman whirled around and Tancred blinked in amazement as a knight on a white horse charged into the square.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Red Knight appears.
paragraphs.simple: A knight in shining chain mail rides into the square on a white horse. He has a helmet with red feathers, a red cloak, a sword with jewels, and a shield with a burning sun on it.

paragraphs.context: Tancred didn't wait for the sword to fall to earth.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Tancred runs to the Pets' Café.
paragraphs.simple: Tancred is amazed and runs off. When he is afraid or excited, he makes wind, and blue and white sparks fly over his head. He runs to Frog Street and calls Mr. Onimous.

background.note: A narrow old street behind the cathedral where the Pets' Café is.

paragraphs.context: Charlie Bone had been fast asleep.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Strange visitors come to the academy at night.
paragraphs.simple: Charlie wakes up and hears voices in the courtyard. He sees Norton Cross, the doorman of the Pets' Café, half carrying a small person in a big hat into the academy.

background.note: The large bouncer who guards the door of the Pets' Café. Only people with pets may enter.
A big bedroom where many pupils sleep. Bloor's pupils sleep at school during the week.

paragraphs.context: The whisper irritated Bragger.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Dagbert wants the window closed.
paragraphs.simple: In the dormitory, Dagbert keeps asking someone to close the window. Bragger is too tired to fight and tells him, "Close it yourself, fish boy!"

background.note: A big, chunky bully at Bloor's Academy, often with Damian Smerk.

paragraphs.context: Tonight the ballroom had been filled with chairs, and Ezekiel Bloor's visitors sat in rows beneath four glittering chandeliers.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Ezekiel holds a secret meeting of bad people.
paragraphs.simple: The old ballroom is full of Ezekiel's guests. They are people who like the dark: thieves, poisoners and kidnappers. The bright lights make them uncomfortable.

background.note: An old street behind the cathedral where the Kettle Shop stands.

paragraphs.context: A glowing circle appeared on the wall.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The guests see Billy in Badlock.
paragraphs.simple: Mrs. Tilpin's mirror shows a picture on the wall: a white-haired boy with thick glasses walks through a jungle with a tiger. It is Billy Raven. A crack runs across the picture because the mirror is broken.

paragraphs.context: At this, Ashkelan pulled his sword from its scabbard and sent it skimming toward the four sisters.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Ashkelan shows how dangerous his sword is.
paragraphs.simple: Ashkelan Kapaldi sends his magic sword flying toward the Yewbeam sisters. They jump up screaming, and the sword stops, standing on its point. It leaves a deep mark in the floor.

background.note: A great swordsman from the 17th century. He is drawn out of his painting to fight for the Bloors' side.

paragraphs.context: Tancred got to his feet.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Uncle Paton finds Tancred.
paragraphs.simple: The person in the dark is Uncle Paton, who always stays out of bright light. His magic makes electric lights explode, which is messy and embarrassing for him.

background.note: Charlie's great-uncle, Grandma Bone's brother. He hides from daylight because his endowment makes lights burst. He helps Charlie.

paragraphs.context: And Titania Tilpin has become the witch she was destined to be.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Paton explains why evil is coming back to the city.
paragraphs.simple: Paton thinks two things have happened at once: Charlie's father came back, and Mrs. Tilpin became a real witch. She is like a channel between the present and Count Harken's world, and she is bringing his helpers into the city.

background.note: An evil enchanter from long ago who married Lilith, the Red King's eldest daughter. He hates the Red King's family.
Titania Tilpin, Joshua's mother. She uses spells and works with the Bloors.
Count Harken's dark, frightening land, reached through a painting.

paragraphs.context: Paton stood up and began to pace the room.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Paton searches for Billy's family.
paragraphs.simple: Paton tells about the box. He looked for Billy's relatives. Billy's aunt would say nothing, but she mentioned Billy's great-uncle, Timothy Raven.

background.note: A small white-haired orphan who lives at Bloor's Academy. He is endowed: he can talk to animals.
Billy Raven's great-uncle.

paragraphs.context: Ezekiel is descended from Maybelle's brother, Bertram, who inherited Septimus's fabulous wealth.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Billy may be the true owner of the Bloor fortune.
paragraphs.simple: Billy comes from Maybelle's family, and Ezekiel comes from her brother Bertram's family. Sally Raven believes Septimus Bloor really left everything to Maybelle and her children, and his true will is hidden in a box.

background.note: The daughter of Septimus Bloor. His true will (1865) left everything to her, but Beatrice, a witch, poisoned her and made a false will.
Ezekiel's great-grandfather. In 1865 he made a will leaving the Bloor house and treasures to his daughter Maybelle.
Maybelle Bloor's brother. Ezekiel Bloor comes from his family.

paragraphs.context: Gabriel Silk had a secret.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Gabriel wants to tell Charlie a secret.
paragraphs.simple: Gabriel cannot find a quiet moment to talk to Charlie, because they are in different dormitories and classes now. He hopes to catch Charlie on the way to a music lesson.

background.note: An endowed music student. He can feel other people's feelings and memories by wearing their clothes. He keeps gerbils.
A dining room. Bloor's has a separate cafeteria for each department, such as the blue cafeteria.

paragraphs.context: A cold shudder ran down Gabriel's spine.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Gabriel notices something strange about a painting.
paragraphs.simple: In the dark hallway, Gabriel thinks a painted gold sword hilt suddenly shone. He feels there is something different and frightening about this painting.

paragraphs.context: The girl turned toward them, and Charlie recognized Olivia Vertigo.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Olivia has white hair now.
paragraphs.simple: Olivia often changes her hair color, but Charlie has never seen it white before. He wonders why she is with Lysander.

background.note: A lively drama student at Bloor's who loves wild clothes and colored hair. She becomes one of Charlie's best friends.
A tall, kind African boy in the art department. He is endowed: he can call up the spirits of his ancestors.

paragraphs.context: Something woke me, I don't know what.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Gabriel tells his secret.
paragraphs.simple: Gabriel saw a hooded man in his yard at night. His father was talking quietly to the man and gave him a package.

paragraphs.context: Charlie had often wondered about the Branko twins.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Branko family is a mystery.
paragraphs.simple: Charlie knows little about the Branko twins. Their family runs a shop called Fine and Fancy, the kind of shop Charlie usually stays away from.

background.note: Telekinetic twin girls at Bloor's Academy, relatives of Zelda Dobinski. They can move things with their minds.
The shop of the Branko family on Spectral Street.

paragraphs.context: Benjamin was almost at the end of Spectral Street when he saw two men on ladders fixing a sign above a shop door.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Brankos' shop gets a new name.
paragraphs.simple: Benjamin sees men putting up a new sign over the shop that used to be called Fine and Fancy. He cannot believe what the new sign says.

background.note: Charlie's best friend, who lives across Filbert Street. He is not endowed and goes to a different school.

paragraphs.context: Gabriel and Benjamin were now regarding Charlie with very puzzled frowns, and Charlie realized he would have to tell them a bit more.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Charlie tells his friends about the box.
paragraphs.simple: Charlie explains that his uncle thinks a box holds a will. The will may prove that Billy Raven should own Bloor's Academy and all the Bloors' money.

paragraphs.context: Charlie felt the smooth painted walls; he knelt and scrutinized the paved floor, running his hands over the colored squares.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Charlie searches for the box.
paragraphs.simple: Charlie looks everywhere in the room: the walls, the floor, the ceiling and the pillars. He finds nothing and wonders if his father hid the box in the castle ruin.

paragraphs.context: Charlie realized that there was no chance of his returning the way he had come.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Amos Byrne chases Charlie with fire.
paragraphs.simple: Charlie must run away from the flames toward the castle. Amos Byrne, the fire-starter, really wants to hurt him.

background.note: A sickly-looking arsonist (a man who starts fires on purpose) who works for the Bloors.

paragraphs.context: Charlie's eyes were open, but his mind was closed to his surroundings, for he was desperately seeking a way of escape.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Red Knight appears again.
paragraphs.simple: Charlie is looking for a way out, and suddenly the knight is there at the end of the tunnel, on his white horse.

paragraphs.context: Losing his terror of the sword, he put on a burst of speed he didn't dream that he had.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Charlie runs toward the knight.
paragraphs.simple: Charlie stops being afraid of the knight's sword and runs very fast. Amos is not afraid of the sword because he trusts his fire.

paragraphs.context: Charlie had often explored the ancient castle.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Charlie looks for a way out through the castle.
paragraphs.simple: Charlie knows the old castle well. The path behind him leads to the glade where the Red King's enchanted tree stands, but he has never gone there from the school grounds.

paragraphs.context: The cats' growling turned to a soft hissing, and they flew away through the woods.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Flames lead Charlie to the wall.
paragraphs.simple: The three Flame cats run through the woods and Charlie follows. He worries about the ten-foot wall between the school grounds and the outside world.

paragraphs.context: With the cats' help he pulled himself up the next few feet.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Charlie climbs the wall.
paragraphs.simple: Charlie remembers where to put his feet and climbs up the wall with the cats' help. He hears the two men chasing him crashing through the trees.

paragraphs.context: Ashkelan must have lost control of the dreadful weapon at last.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Charlie gets home safely.
paragraphs.simple: The magic sword stops following Charlie. Maybe it can only move when it is near its owner. Charlie is tired and has a pain in his side, but he is alive. The Flames take him to number nine.

background.note: Three magic copper-colored cats, Aries, Leo and Sagittarius, who protect Charlie and the good endowed children.

paragraphs.context: The silence lasted only a few seconds, but in that time so many thoughts swept through Charlie's head, he began to feel dizzy.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Charlie thinks about Billy and the box.
paragraphs.simple: Charlie thinks of Billy lost in the enchanter's forest, and of a wooden box decorated with mother-of-pearl. The secret in it could change everyone's lives.

paragraphs.context: Venetia unlocked the door and led the way into a dark hall.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Charlie goes into Venetia's house.
paragraphs.simple: The hall has a strong, bitter smell. A long rack is full of clothes, and Charlie remembers that Venetia can bewitch people with clothes.

background.note: The youngest great-aunt, Grandma Bone's sister. She is vain and makes dangerous enchanted clothes.

paragraphs.context: Having prodded her grandson into a chair at the table, Grandma Bone and her sisters began arguing over the seating arrangements.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Charlie has to sit with his enemies.
paragraphs.simple: The sisters argue about where everyone sits. Charlie must sit opposite Manfred and next to Eustacia, who is going to use her magic powers.

background.note: Dr. Bloor's son and head boy of Bloor's Academy. He is endowed: he can hypnotize people. He is cruel to Charlie.
Charlie's grandmother, his father's mother. She was born a Yewbeam. She is cold and bossy and spies on Charlie.
The middle great-aunt, Grandma Bone's sister. She has an iron-gray bun and sometimes sees the future.
The eldest of Charlie's three great-aunts, Grandma Bone's sister. She is a strict, unkind woman.

paragraphs.context: He felt as though he were falling into them.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Manfred hypnotizes Charlie.
paragraphs.simple: Charlie tries not to look into Manfred's dark eyes, but he cannot stop the pictures in his head. He sees the boat Greywing on a stormy sea under a sky full of stars. Charlie fears that now his enemies know where his parents are.

background.note: The boat Charlie's parents sail in.

paragraphs.context: He did not seem to be wholly engaged with the conversation around the table.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Something else is worrying Uncle Paton.
paragraphs.simple: Paton says the right things about Charlie's story, but Charlie feels his uncle is thinking about something else.

paragraphs.context: The huge Sea Globe now stood in the center of the ballroom.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Sea Globe is shown in the ballroom.
paragraphs.simple: The Sea Globe is in a glass box. It is a glowing ball of moving water showing the oceans and the land of the world.

background.note: Lord Grimwald's huge globe of blue-green sea water, kept in a big glass box at Bloor's Academy.

paragraphs.context: Lord Grimwald smiled with satisfaction.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Lord Grimwald talks about the Sea Globe.
paragraphs.simple: Lord Grimwald says an ancestor long ago pulled water out of the Northern Sea into his arms and made the globe. Through it, Lord Grimwald can control the oceans.

background.note: Dagbert's father, a powerful, frightening man who can control the oceans.

paragraphs.context: He gazed up at the water tumbling far above him in the Arctic Ocean.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Joshua looks at the Sea Globe.
paragraphs.simple: Joshua stares at the water in the globe. The blue-green light makes even his mother and Manfred look better.

background.note: A strange new boy with paper stuck in his hair. He is endowed with magnetism: things and people are drawn to him.

paragraphs.context: "Believe me, you will attract gold if you think about it.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Lord Grimwald gives Joshua advice.
paragraphs.simple: Joshua has the power of magnetism: things stick to him. Lord Grimwald tells him that the mind is important in magnetism, and that he can make the dirt on his sweater go away by thinking.

paragraphs.context: This was not an endearment, although the doctor was very fond of Cook.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Cook's real name is Treasure.
paragraphs.simple: Cook goes to her secret room, where Dr. Saltweather is waiting. He calls her "Treasure". It is not a loving word here: Treasure really is her name.

background.note: Cook's real first name. Here it is a name, not the word 'treasure'.

paragraphs.context: No one else to look after her.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Cook hurries away from the academy.
paragraphs.simple: Cook tells Mrs. Weedon she is visiting a sick friend. Then she hurries into the old part of the city.

background.note: The cook at Bloor's Academy. She is kind to the children and secretly helps Charlie and his friends.
The quiet square by the cathedral where Miss Ingledew's bookshop stands, at Number Three.
The gardener and porter at Bloor's Academy. He works for the Bloors and is not friendly to the children.

paragraphs.context: "I had some very important customers and they didn't leave until half past six," Miss Ingledew explained, distractedly lifting her mug of cocoa to her lips.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Two men break into the bookshop.
paragraphs.simple: Miss Ingledew explains that two villains pushed their way into her shop just as she was closing.

background.note: Julia Ingledew, the kind owner of a bookshop near the cathedral. Uncle Paton likes her very much.

paragraphs.context: "I feel I should go there tonight."
paragraphs.mainIdea: Miss Ingledew worries about Charlie.
paragraphs.simple: Miss Ingledew wants to go to Charlie's house, but Grandma Bone would stop her. She cannot phone either, and Paton never answers his cell phone.

paragraphs.context: As Olivia drew closer to her home, she began to think about her godmother, Alice Angel.
paragraphs.mainIdea: We meet Olivia's godmother, Alice Angel.
paragraphs.simple: Alice has a flower shop in Steppingstones. She helped Olivia find her endowment and always knows when Olivia needs her. Alice is a white witch, a good witch.

background.note: A mysterious, gentle woman with green eyes who runs a flower shop. She seems to know all about Charlie's friends.

paragraphs.context: A white rose dropped from its stalk, and then another and another.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Alice knows something has happened to Olivia.
paragraphs.simple: Alice's fresh flowers suddenly lose all their petals, like a storm of snow. She knows Olivia is in trouble.

paragraphs.context: Charlie sat in the kitchen, eating oatmeal.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Emma tells Charlie the news.
paragraphs.simple: Charlie is very tired. Emma tells him about the men at her aunt's shop and describes the Sea Globe, as Cook told it.

paragraphs.context: Every contact I had seems to have gone dead.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Paton cannot reach Charlie's father.
paragraphs.simple: Uncle Paton has no way to reach Lyell. The harbormaster has left and a ship's captain has disappeared, but there is still a little hope.

background.note: Lyell Bone, Charlie's father. For years he was under a spell, but now he is free. He and Charlie's mother are away at sea.

paragraphs.context: They climbed in single file, their footsteps echoing in the confined space, the only sound for miles, it seemed.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The children climb Tigerfield Steps.
paragraphs.simple: The friends go up the steps one behind another. Charlie reads the numbers on the old oak doors; some are missing.

paragraphs.context: A police car arrived soon after the ambulance.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Barnaby Bittermouse is dead.
paragraphs.simple: The police and an ambulance come, but the old man is dead. It looks like a robbery, but his wallet and gold watch are still there.

paragraphs.context: Uncle Paton's dark eyes never left his sister's face as he slowly stirred the spoon around and around in his cup.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Paton accuses Grandma Bone.
paragraphs.simple: Paton says Grandma Bone is part of a plan to cheat Billy Raven out of his inheritance, even if it means drowning her own son.

paragraphs.context: Maisie came into the room just as Paton was about to run and fetch her.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Maisie welcomes Alice.
paragraphs.simple: Maisie listens to Alice's story. Soon she likes Olivia's godmother and makes up a bed for her.

background.note: Charlie's other grandmother, his mother's mother. She is warm, noisy and loving, and lives with Charlie's family.

paragraphs.context: Before Billy could think what might be coming next, two guards stepped forward and grabbed his arms.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Billy is taken to the dungeons.
paragraphs.simple: In Badlock, guards take Billy away to the dungeons. His rat Rembrandt runs after him, and Matilda cries out against it.

background.note: A black rat. First Mr. Boldova's pet, later Billy Raven's. He can talk to Billy.
Count Harken and Lilith's lonely young granddaughter in Badlock. She becomes Billy Raven's friend.

paragraphs.context: Charlie sniffed the cold air and agreed with her.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Charlie gets ready for school.
paragraphs.simple: The morning air smells fresh. Charlie is glad of his warm blue school cape, although children in the street sometimes laugh at it.

paragraphs.context: Lysander and Gabriel were already immersed in their work.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Gabriel is worried about Olivia.
paragraphs.simple: In homework time, Gabriel rolls his eyes toward Olivia to show Charlie that something is wrong with her. They talk without words.

paragraphs.context: Trying to look casual but putting on speed whenever he thought no one was looking, Charlie hurried after Joshua.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Charlie follows Joshua into the ruin.
paragraphs.simple: Joshua goes under the great red arch and disappears. Charlie stands in front of five small arches that lead into the ruin.

paragraphs.context: The knight removed his gauntlet and laid a bare hand on the white mare's neck, calming her instantly.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Charlie wonders who the Red Knight is.
paragraphs.simple: The knight calms his horse and turns to Charlie. Charlie looks at the dark eye holes in the helmet and wonders if he knows the face behind it.

paragraphs.context: Only Joshua saw what really happened to the swordsman's body.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Joshua sees the swordsman's body disappear.
paragraphs.simple: A snowy mist fills the glade, full of the sounds of an old battle. Only Joshua sees what happens to Ashkelan's body.

paragraphs.context: Gabriel was the last person to leave the coatroom.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Charlie goes secretly into the music tower.
paragraphs.simple: When the hall is empty, Charlie runs to the tower door. But Dorcas Loom comes out of the green coatroom and sees the door closing.

background.note: A plump, cheerful-looking endowed girl at Bloor's Academy.
A room where pupils keep their capes and coats. Each department has one, such as the blue coatroom.

paragraphs.context: Now he could see them: Lysander's spirit ancestors.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Lysander's spirit ancestors come to help.
paragraphs.simple: Tall dark warriors stand all along the walls, with gold on their necks and arms, white robes, spears and burning torches. They are the spirits of Lysander's African ancestors.

paragraphs.context: Once more Charlie felt them drift past him.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The spirit warriors leave.
paragraphs.simple: After Lord Grimwald screams, the spirit warriors slowly move back. Their torches die and their white robes turn into steam. Charlie stares at the Sea Globe.

paragraphs.context: No one seemed to notice their late arrival in the dining hall.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Charlie and Lysander come in late.
paragraphs.simple: The teachers sit on a high platform to watch the students, but today they are busy eating, so nobody sees the boys come in.

paragraphs.context: She wasn't herself, he could see that.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Olivia is bewitched by a vest.
paragraphs.simple: Olivia looks ill and unfriendly. Charlie sees something glittery under her cape and understands: it is a bewitched vest.

paragraphs.context: By the time he had finished, Emma's spirits had risen considerably.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Emma feels hopeful again.
paragraphs.simple: Charlie's news makes Emma much happier. She thinks they can win, and that Olivia will be herself again if they take the awful vest away.

paragraphs.context: He hadn't visited Cook's apartment for some time, but shining his flashlight across the rows of closets, he quickly recognized Cook's entrance.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Charlie goes to Cook's secret rooms.
paragraphs.simple: In the dark kitchen, Charlie finds the closet door that leads to Cook's secret apartment. If the Bloors find out about it, Cook will be sent away.

paragraphs.context: Her tone was soft and sly, and they looked at her uneasily.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mrs. Tilpin says Harken is coming.
paragraphs.simple: Mrs. Tilpin says that nothing has really changed, because Count Harken is coming and his people are already in the city. She dances around the pool.

paragraphs.context: Billy's bed was now a bale of prickly straw, his light a thin candle that always burned through before nightfall.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Billy is in a dungeon in Badlock.
paragraphs.simple: Billy's cell has no windows, only straw to sleep on and a small candle. At least he can talk to his rat, Rembrandt.

paragraphs.context: Billy had refused to be rescued by Charlie.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Billy is sorry he stayed in Badlock.
paragraphs.simple: Billy thought life in Badlock would be better, with animals and a friend, Matilda. After a week in the dungeons he wants to go home, but he thinks Charlie will not come again.

paragraphs.context: One day while she was hiding, she had heard a woman's voice coming from the painting of Billy's city.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Matilda learns about Titania.
paragraphs.simple: Matilda heard a woman's voice coming from a painting of Billy's city, and the enchanter answered it. So she knows that a woman called Titania is helping Count Harken get into the city.

paragraphs.context: Alice dropped the book she had been dusting and ran down the two flights of stairs.
paragraphs.mainIdea: A wet stranger arrives.
paragraphs.simple: Alice hears a scream and runs downstairs. In the kitchen sits a man in a waterproof hat and raincoat, with a big brown mustache, all dripping.

paragraphs.context: Tancred shuddered and made a dash for the Kettle Shop.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Tancred goes to the Kettle Shop.
paragraphs.simple: Tancred rings and rings the bell of the Kettle Shop. A gang of pale teenagers laughs at him when his false mustache falls off.

background.note: Mrs. Kettle's shop on Piminy Street, which sells kettles. Its door knocker is a little bronze kettle.

paragraphs.context: Charlie quickly explained his idea for releasing Olivia from her bewitching.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Charlie has a plan to help Olivia.
paragraphs.simple: Alice likes Charlie's idea. She asks Emma to describe the bewitched vest in every detail.

paragraphs.context: But she called because Dagbert will only speak to you, Charlie.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Dagbert asks for Charlie.
paragraphs.simple: Miss Ingledew phones: Mrs. Kettle and Tancred are at the bookstore, and Dagbert wants to speak only to Charlie.

background.note: A strong, friendly woman who runs the Kettle Shop on Piminy Street and is Cook's good friend.

paragraphs.context: Dagbert turned the sea storm over and over in his hands.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Dagbert is free of his fear.
paragraphs.simple: Dagbert looks at the sea storm and says his fear is gone. He is not afraid that his life will end anymore, and he gives Charlie a happy smile.

paragraphs.context: Tancred volunteered to walk with them as far as High Street.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The boys leave the bookstore.
paragraphs.simple: Emma watches the three boys walk away down Cathedral Close. Tancred waves and almost blows her a kiss.

paragraphs.context: As she closed the spare room's door, she felt a pang of guilt.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Alice worries about giving Charlie hope.
paragraphs.simple: Alice told Charlie about a distant girl. Now she worries that this has given him false hope.

paragraphs.context: Emma had gone to bed feeling useless.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Emma cannot sleep.
paragraphs.simple: Emma worries about Olivia, Tancred and her aunt. She also wonders if Count Harken could really surround the city with his magic.

paragraphs.context: The sight of the three tall houses always made Emma shudder.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Emma flies to Darkly Wynd.
paragraphs.simple: As a bird, Emma flies to Darkly Wynd, where the Yewbeam sisters live. She wonders which house has the mirror.

background.note: A dark, narrow alley where the three Yewbeam aunts live, at number thirteen.

paragraphs.context: Emma fluttered down to the sill and peered into the room beyond.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Emma finds Venetia's workroom.
paragraphs.simple: Through a dirty window, Emma sees a table covered with cloth, bottles of colored liquid and piles of sequins. It is where Venetia makes bewitched clothes.

paragraphs.context: Charlie sat back in the chair and gazed at the mirror.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Emma has brought the mirror, but it is broken.
paragraphs.simple: Charlie wonders how Emma found Amoret's mirror. It is still cracked, so he thinks he cannot use it to get into Badlock.

paragraphs.context: But now the moth was busily skimming over the cracked glass.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Claerwen mends the mirror.
paragraphs.simple: Charlie's moth, Claerwen, moves quickly over the broken glass of Amoret's mirror. Bright light begins to stream out of it.

paragraphs.context: A journey with Amoret's mirror was nothing like traveling through a painting.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Charlie travels to Badlock with the mirror.
paragraphs.simple: On the way, Charlie sees pictures he will never forget: golden sand hills, a camel with a tiny boy, cities with domes, and a deep blue sea.

background.note: The Red King's youngest child, a daughter born just before the queen died.

paragraphs.context: A head of brown bristles was revealed, rather like a hedgehog's spines.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Charlie is disguised as a servant.
paragraphs.simple: Dorgo gives Charlie his cap and his brown robe. Matilda helps Charlie hide his hair under the big cap.

background.note: A small servant in Count Harken's palace who speaks broken English.

paragraphs.context: Charlie tore down the rest of the steps, stumbling and slipping on the rocky surface.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Charlie finds Billy's cell.
paragraphs.simple: At the bottom of the steps is a room with a candle. Behind the bars of a cell, a small figure lies on a bed of straw.

paragraphs.context: I suppose I was silly to like it so much in Badlock.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Billy is glad to be home.
paragraphs.simple: Billy says the count was nice to him at first and made animals for him. But the animals had no hearts, and later he was put in the dungeon.

paragraphs.context: The mayor and some of the councillors had left the city.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The city is closing down.
paragraphs.simple: Many people have left. Only a few police officers are on the streets, schools and banks are closed, and there are no taxis.

background.note: A police officer in the city.

paragraphs.context: There were few to see the dark figure striding up the road; his magnificence was wasted on the creatures of the night, who quickly fled.
paragraphs.mainIdea: A grand, frightening stranger comes.
paragraphs.simple: A man in a gold cloak with emeralds and pearls walks up the road at night. Even the night animals run away from him. It is Count Harken.

paragraphs.context: The huge brass gong hung in an oak frame outside the headmaster's study.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The great gong is to be rung.
paragraphs.simple: The count wants a gong rung to wake everyone. Weedon has never dared to hit this big brass gong. Once Manfred hit it so hard in a bad temper that the hammer broke.

paragraphs.context: "That's the only moment in the whole day when she'll take it off," said Emma.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Emma plans to change Olivia's vest.
paragraphs.simple: Mrs. Kettle makes Emma feel brave. Emma plans to go to Olivia's house and switch the bewitched vest for Alice's new one while Olivia is dressing.

paragraphs.context: Bounding into the kitchen, she ran straight into Dagbert Endless, who was getting himself a drink of water.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mrs. Kettle arrives invisible.
paragraphs.simple: Mrs. Kettle is wearing the blue boa, which makes her invisible. She surprises Dagbert in the bookstore kitchen and stops him from screaming.

paragraphs.context: During the night the fog crept right over the city in a smothering gray cloud.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Fog covers the city.
paragraphs.simple: Thick fog lies over the city. The wild people of Piminy Street sleep in the streets among broken glass and ash. Everyone waits in fear.

paragraphs.context: Olivia was now humming monotonously as she washed her hair.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Emma switches the vests.
paragraphs.simple: While Olivia washes her hair, Emma finds the bewitched vest and puts the new one in its place. Her hand shakes, because she does not know what Olivia will do.

paragraphs.context: A little later he became aware that two more people had joined their ranks.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Teachers join the children.
paragraphs.simple: As the group walks through the city, Dr. Saltweather and Señor Alvaro come to help them.

background.note: The white-haired head of the music department at Bloor's Academy. He teaches brass and choir.

paragraphs.context: And then, from somewhere behind them, a rock came hurtling through the air.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Piminy Street gang attacks.
paragraphs.simple: A rock hits Dagbert. Charlie sees a row of wild people on the road, with slingshots, clubs and knives.

paragraphs.context: She dug her claws deep into his shoulder.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Alice saves Charlie from Mrs. Tilpin.
paragraphs.simple: The witch attacks Charlie. Then Alice Angel sends a beam of pure white light into Mrs. Tilpin's eyes.

paragraphs.context: And then Charlie saw on the other side of the field a mounted knight in shining armor.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Green Knight appears.
paragraphs.simple: The enchanter comes as a knight in a green cloak, on a black stallion that breathes fire.

paragraphs.context: With all his strength he leaped for the stallion's harness, dragging at its head.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Red Knight kills the enchanter.
paragraphs.simple: Charlie pulls at the black horse. At that moment the Red Knight's sword goes into the Green Knight's heart.

background.note: A mysterious knight in a red cloak and a silver helmet with red feathers, who comes to help Charlie.

paragraphs.context: He lay on his back, only a few feet away.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Red Knight is badly hurt.
paragraphs.simple: The Red Knight lies on the ground, bleeding, and his white horse stands over him. Charlie runs to him.

paragraphs.context: Lyell Bone was lifted onto a stretcher and carried to an ambulance.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Red Knight was Charlie's father.
paragraphs.simple: Charlie's father, Lyell, is taken to hospital, and Charlie goes with him. Officer Singh looks at Charlie with special interest.

paragraphs.context: The wild strangers that had invaded Piminy Street seemed to have vanished as mysteriously as they had arrived.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Piminy Street is quiet again.
paragraphs.simple: The wild strangers have gone. Mrs. Kettle hangs her great sword back on the wall, and the blue boa lives among the kettles again.

background.note: A blue boa constrictor snake that once belonged to the Red King. Its hug makes people invisible.

paragraphs.context: He would have to take the matter to court, of course, but the judge thought Lyell stood an excellent chance of winning his case.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The will is good news for Charlie's family.
paragraphs.simple: A wise judge says that Lyell Bone is the true heir to Septimus Bloor's fortune. Lyell must still go to court, but he will probably win.

paragraphs.context: So Billy went up to the Silks' home in the Heights.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Billy finds a new home for a while.
paragraphs.simple: Billy stays with Benjamin first, but Rembrandt hates Runner Bean, so Billy moves to the Silks' house, where there are many pets.

background.note: Benjamin's big, friendly yellow dog. He often helps Charlie and his friends.
Charlie's first friend at Bloor's Academy, a music student from a big musical family. He is not endowed.
Onoria Onimous, Mr. Onimous's tall, gentle wife with a very long nose. She makes the cakes at the Pets' Café.
A rich part of the city on a wooded hill, where many Bloor's pupils live.

paragraphs.context: After too much food, Rembrandt fell asleep and slipped off Billy's lap.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The book ends with a happy party.
paragraphs.simple: At the Pets' Café party, Billy goes under the table to save Rembrandt from Runner Bean. He comes up grinning and tells Charlie that Tancred and Emma are holding hands.

paragraphs.context: Charlie smiled to himself in the dark and whispered
paragraphs.mainIdea: Charlie calls Fidelio by a dog's name.
paragraphs.simple: Fidelio has just told Dagbert to stop shouting. Charlie smiles and whispers, "Well done, Fido!" Fido is a name people give a dog. Fidelio and Fido sound alike, so Charlie is praising his friend with a joke name.

sentences.context: He ran across to the green door and, pulling a key from his pocket, shakily inserted it into the lock.
sentences.simple: He ran to the green door, took a key out of his pocket and put it in the lock with shaking hands.
sentences.main: He put the key in the lock.

parts.text: He ran across to the green door
parts.meaning: He ran over to the green door

parts.text: and, pulling a key from his pocket,
parts.meaning: and, taking a key out of his pocket,

parts.text: shakily inserted it into the lock.
parts.meaning: put it into the lock with shaking hands.

sentences.grammar: The -ing clause "pulling a key..." happens just before the main verb "inserted".

sentences.context: The knocking had ceased at last and, peering through the cafe window, Tancred caught a glimpse of two figures walking down the alley.
sentences.simple: The knocking stopped, and through the window Tancred saw two people walking down the alley.

parts.text: The knocking had ceased at last
parts.meaning: The knocking had finally stopped

parts.text: and, peering through the cafe window,
parts.meaning: and, looking carefully through the café window,

parts.text: Tancred caught a glimpse of two figures walking down the alley.
parts.meaning: Tancred quickly saw two people going down the narrow street.

sentences.grammar: "Catch a glimpse of" means see for a very short time.

sentences.context: It was several minutes before Tancred could bring himself to move again, and by the time he emerged on High Street, the two figures were nowhere to be seen.
sentences.simple: Tancred could not move for several minutes, and when he got to High Street the two people had gone.

parts.text: It was several minutes before Tancred could bring himself to move again,
parts.meaning: For several minutes Tancred could not make himself move,

parts.text: and by the time he emerged on High Street,
parts.meaning: and when he came out onto High Street,

parts.text: the two figures were nowhere to be seen.
parts.meaning: the two people had disappeared.

sentences.grammar: "Bring yourself to do something" means make yourself do it. "Nowhere to be seen" means not seen anywhere.

sentences.context: Tancred had been about to run from the scene, but he stood rooted to the spot, scarcely able to believe his eyes.
sentences.simple: Tancred was going to run away, but he could not move because he could hardly believe what he saw.
sentences.main: Tancred stood rooted to the spot.

parts.text: Tancred had been about to run from the scene,
parts.meaning: Tancred was just going to run away,

parts.text: but he stood rooted to the spot,
parts.meaning: but he could not move,

parts.text: scarcely able to believe his eyes.
parts.meaning: almost unable to believe what he saw.

sentences.grammar: "Rooted to the spot" means not able to move, like a tree. "Scarcely" means almost not.

sentences.context: Ezekiel Bloor's white, waxy hair framed a face so gaunt and bony, it looked more like a skull than the face of a living person.
sentences.simple: Ezekiel's face was so thin and bony that it looked like a skull.
sentences.main: His face looked like a skull.

parts.text: Ezekiel Bloor's white, waxy hair framed a face
parts.meaning: Ezekiel Bloor's white, shiny hair was around a face

parts.text: so gaunt and bony,
parts.meaning: that was so thin and bony

parts.text: it looked more like a skull than the face of a living person.
parts.meaning: that it looked like the bones of a dead head, not a living face.

sentences.grammar: "So ... (that) ..." shows a result; here "that" is left out.

sentences.context: It contained ancient, dusty books bound in peeling leather, their yellowed leaves covered in mysterious, faded writing.
sentences.simple: There were very old, dusty books with old leather covers and yellow pages full of strange, faded writing.

parts.text: It contained ancient, dusty books
parts.meaning: There were very old, dusty books in it

parts.text: bound in peeling leather,
parts.meaning: with leather covers that were coming off,

parts.text: their yellowed leaves covered in mysterious, faded writing.
parts.meaning: and their yellow pages had strange, pale writing on them.

sentences.grammar: "Leaves" here means pages. The last part has no verb; it adds a picture of the books.

sentences.context: The man had shoulder-length black hair, and between the black mustache and pointed beard, his fleshy lips held an unpleasant grin.
sentences.simple: The man had black hair to his shoulders, a black mustache and pointed beard, and an unpleasant smile.
sentences.main: The man had an unpleasant grin.

parts.text: The man had shoulder-length black hair,
parts.meaning: The man's black hair reached his shoulders,

parts.text: and between the black mustache and pointed beard,
parts.meaning: and between his black mustache and pointed beard,

parts.text: his fleshy lips held an unpleasant grin.
parts.meaning: his thick lips showed a nasty smile.

sentences.grammar: This describes the man in the painting. "Held a grin" is a written way to say "smiled".

sentences.context: The small yard in front of the cafe was crammed with chairs, cupboards, tables, boxes, and a large iron bedstead.
sentences.simple: The little yard in front of the café was full of furniture and boxes.
sentences.main: The yard was full of things.

parts.text: The small yard in front of the cafe
parts.meaning: The little yard in front of the café

parts.text: was crammed with
parts.meaning: was very full of

parts.text: chairs, cupboards, tables, boxes, and a large iron bedstead.
parts.meaning: chairs, cupboards, tables, boxes, and a big iron bed frame.

sentences.grammar: "Crammed with" means so full that there is no more room.

sentences.context: The ground was paved with tiny squares of color: yellow, red, and orange, a mosaic of a burning sun.
sentences.simple: The floor was made of tiny colored squares that made a picture of a burning sun.
sentences.main: The ground was paved with tiny squares.

parts.text: The ground was paved with tiny squares of color:
parts.meaning: The floor was covered with tiny colored stones:

parts.text: yellow, red, and orange,
parts.meaning: yellow, red, and orange,

parts.text: a mosaic of a burning sun.
parts.meaning: making a picture of a burning sun.

sentences.grammar: A "mosaic" is a picture made from many small pieces. The burning sun is the Red King's sign.

sentences.context: They came, at last, to the wide expanse of grass that lay between the school and the woods that surrounded the castle.
sentences.simple: At last they reached the large area of grass between the school and the woods around the castle.

parts.text: They came, at last,
parts.meaning: Finally they arrived

parts.text: to the wide expanse of grass
parts.meaning: at the large open area of grass

parts.text: that lay between the school and the woods that surrounded the castle.
parts.meaning: that was between the school and the woods around the castle.

sentences.grammar: "Expanse" means a wide open area. Two "that" clauses describe the grass and the woods.

sentences.context: His head twisted this way and that, and his right hand swung back and forth across his body, as though he were orchestrating the movements of an army.
sentences.simple: He turned his head from side to side and moved his right hand across his body, as if he were directing an army.
sentences.main: He moved as if he were leading an army.

parts.text: His head twisted this way and that,
parts.meaning: He turned his head from side to side,

parts.text: and his right hand swung back and forth across his body,
parts.meaning: and his right hand moved back and forward in front of him,

parts.text: as though he were orchestrating the movements of an army.
parts.meaning: as if he were directing a whole army.

sentences.grammar: "Orchestrate" means organize carefully, like a conductor with an orchestra. "As though he were" is an unreal comparison.

sentences.context: Joshua's thin hair was covered in bits of paper, crumbs and pencil shavings clung to his sweater, and his shoes were coated with dead leaves and mud.
sentences.simple: Joshua had paper in his hair, crumbs and pencil bits on his sweater, and leaves and mud on his shoes.

parts.text: Joshua's thin hair was covered in bits of paper,
parts.meaning: Joshua's thin hair had bits of paper on it,

parts.text: crumbs and pencil shavings clung to his sweater,
parts.meaning: crumbs and bits from sharpened pencils stuck to his sweater,

parts.text: and his shoes were coated with dead leaves and mud.
parts.meaning: and his shoes were covered with dead leaves and mud.

sentences.grammar: Joshua's magnetism makes things stick to him. "Cling to" means stick to.

sentences.context: The man beside him looked down as from a great height, and Joshua noted the crinkled, almost green hair, the chilly arctic eyes, and the grayish glimmering skin.
sentences.simple: The very tall man looked down at Joshua, who saw his wavy, almost green hair, his cold eyes and his gray, shining skin.

parts.meaning: The man next to him looked down as if from very high up,

parts.text: and Joshua noted
parts.meaning: and Joshua noticed

parts.text: the crinkled, almost green hair, the chilly arctic eyes, and the grayish glimmering skin.
parts.meaning: the wavy, almost green hair, the very cold eyes, and the gray, shining skin.

sentences.grammar: "As from" means "as if from". Lord Grimwald looks like the cold sea.

sentences.context: Two shelves had collapsed, the ladder that was used to reach the highest shelves was broken, and the cash register had been turned on its side.
sentences.simple: Two shelves had fallen, the ladder was broken, and the cash register was lying on its side.

parts.text: Two shelves had collapsed,
parts.meaning: Two shelves had fallen down,

parts.text: the ladder that was used to reach the highest shelves was broken,
parts.meaning: the ladder for the top shelves was broken,

parts.text: and the cash register had been turned on its side.
parts.meaning: and someone had pushed the cash register over onto its side.

sentences.grammar: Past perfect ("had collapsed") shows what had happened before the person saw it.

sentences.context: Today she chose a scarlet dress to wear over her tight black jeans, a white scarf with a glittering fringe, a fur-lined denim jacket, and a black felt hat.
sentences.simple: Today she wore a bright red dress over black jeans, a white scarf, a warm denim jacket and a black hat.

parts.meaning: Today she picked a bright red dress

parts.text: to wear over her tight black jeans,
parts.meaning: to put on over her tight black jeans,

parts.text: a white scarf with a glittering fringe, a fur-lined denim jacket, and a black felt hat.
parts.meaning: a white scarf with shiny ends, a jeans jacket with fur inside, and a black felt hat.

sentences.grammar: "Scarlet" is a bright red color. The list continues the object of "chose".

sentences.context: His throat felt tight, his ears buzzed, and the icy foreboding that clutched at his stomach got worse and worse.

parts.text: and the icy foreboding that clutched at his stomach got worse and worse.

sentences.grammar: "Foreboding" is a feeling that something bad will happen. "Worse and worse" shows a growing change.

sentences.context: He would have to sit beneath a light, several lights most probably, and every one of them would explode, to Paton's utter humiliation and embarrassment.

sentences.context: A pot of tea had been made, oatmeal was cooking on the stove, and slices of golden-brown toast filled the toast rack on the table.
